text.p: The surprise callup of AC Milan star Roberto Baggio to Italy's World Cup squad by Italian coach Cesare Maldini on Thursday could represent a turning point for both men.
For Baggio, the recall to the national team could mark a welcome change of fortune in an apparently declining career.

For Maldini, the decision to recall a player so manifestly overlooked in recent seasons by predecessor Arrigo Sacchi would seem to indicate his growing self-confidence in the hot seat of Italian soccer.
The 30-year-old Baggio has won 45 caps but last played for Italy in a September 1995, 1-0 European Championship win over Slovenia.

Arguably the most famous Italian player of his generation, Baggio's status reached that of national hero following the 1994 World Cup finals where he scored five goals during Italy's run to final before they lost on penalties to Brazil.
Since that final, however, Baggio has played only twice for Italy, in a 2-1 European Championship defeat by Croatia in Palermo in November 1994 and against Slovenia.
Persistent injury problems since the '94 finals in the United States apparently undermined Sacchi's confidence in him, leading commentators to speculate that Baggio's international career was over.
Now fully fit, Baggio has ironically again found himself blocked by Sacchi following the coach's decision last December to resign the Italy job in order to return to AC Milan.
There he has appeared to favour Marco Simone, Frenchman Christophe Dugarry or Montenegrin Dejan Savicevic to partner automatic first-choice striker George Weah of Liberia.
Sacchi did, however, relent for Milan's last two games, picking Baggio from the start for a 3-1 defeat by Internazionale and a 0-0 draw with Piacenza.

Baggio recently reiterated his desire to get back into the national squad in order to play at the France'98 World Cup finals, adding that if necessary he would leave Milan in order to refloat his career.

"My wish is to stay at Milan, but only to play...Next season, I've got to play (regularly) in order to win my way back into the France '98 World Cup side, I simply cannot sit on the bench all season as has happened this year".
Spanish sides Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid and English clubs Aston Villa and Blackburn have all made reported enquiries about Baggio, who currently has an estimated $20 million dollar price tag.

Baggio's call-up for Wednesday's World Cup qualifier against Poland in Naples is prompted partly by concern about the fitness of Chelsea striker Gianfranco Zola, who is struggling with muscular problems.
With Juventus schemer Alessandro Del Piero also injured, coach Maldini had little option but to turn to Baggio if he wanted a player similar to Zola.
The Chelsea man is expected to recover in time for next week's game but Baggio's inclusion in the squad leaves open the possibility of a second-half appearance as substitute for Zola.
Italy currently lead group two on 13 points, four clear of second-placed England who have a game in hand.
Maldini's recall of Baggio will inevitably prompt comparisons between the philosophies of the past and present Italian national coaches,.
Since taking over from Sacchi in December, Maldini has been at pains to avoid criticizing to his predecessor.
His decision to summon a player systematically overlooked by Sacchi both at international and club level indicates that Maldini places greater emphasis on traditional Italian flair than did Sacchi.
Throughout his five years as Italy coach, Sacchi was constantly slated for imposing too rigid a tactical discipline on his players, thus stifling instinctive skills.
In contrast, Maldini once said that there are no such things as "playmakers" or "schemers" in soccer, merely "good players".
Presumably, Maldini believes that Baggio is a good player.
